title: Lectures or Group Decision
text:
During World War II, meat was rationed in the United States, and the government wanted families to eat cuts that were nutritious and available but unpopular, such as beef hearts, kidneys and sweetbreads. Kurt Lewin, a German emigre psychologist then at the University of Iowa, ran a study to find the best way to change these habits.

He worked with groups of women volunteers who ran their households. Some groups heard an attractive lecture by an expert explaining the nutritional value of these meats, the wartime need, and giving recipes. Other groups of similar size were given the same information by a leader, but instead of listening to a lecture, they discussed it among themselves. At the end, they were asked to indicate, by raising their hands, whether they intended to try serving one of these meats.

Later follow-up showed a striking difference. Only about 3 percent of women who heard a lecture reported serving one of the meats. Among those who took part in the discussion and group decision, about 32 percent did.

Lewin concluded that changing habits is easier when people decide together, as a group, than when they are told what to do as individuals.
lesson: People change more when they decide together than when they are lectured. Give your team the facts, then let them discuss and commit as a group.
location: University of Iowa, Iowa City, Iowa, USA
source: Lewin, K. (1947). Group decision and social change. In T. M. Newcomb and E. L. Hartley (Eds.), Readings in Social Psychology. Henry Holt.
caveat: The groups were small and the study was loosely controlled, so public commitment and other factors may have contributed to the effect.
